headline: Author manually justified 17,000 words in a Super Metroid guide by careful word choice
summary: A guide author achieved perfect right-justified text in monospace for 17,000 words by meticulously selecting words to avoid double spaces and ensure every line ended precisely on a letter.
details: In a remarkable feat of dedication, a guide author named rs1n manually justified 17,000 words for their Super Metroid guide in the late 1990s. This involved meticulously choosing every word to ensure perfect right alignment on each line, without a single double space.

Typesetting in monospace presents unique challenges for justification, as fixed-width characters make even spacing difficult. Centering is tricky, and full justification often results in unpleasantly large and uneven spaces, making hyphenation the usual but imperfect solution.

rs1n's method was simple yet arduous: 'I just chose words carefully so that everything lined up on the right hand side.' This entire 17,000-word guide was crafted using only an ASCII editor, highlighting an extraordinary level of precision and patience.

While a curiosity, this dedication resonates with anyone who has spent hours adjusting text to fit specific width constraints in user interfaces. It's a testament to the lengths creators go for aesthetic perfection, even in seemingly simple text formats.

headline_marked: [[Phishing Site Tried to Talk to My AI]], becoming evidence for takedown
headline: Phishing Site Tried to Talk to My AI, becoming evidence for takedown
summary: A developer built an AI agent to detect phishing by identifying hidden instructions meant to trick the AI itself. This adversarial interaction became the strongest evidence for takedown.
details: A developer created Sentinel, a fleet of specialized AI agents on Google Cloud, to combat phishing. This system monitors real-time Certificate Transparency logs, which generate millions of certificates daily, to identify new phishing domains.

Traditional phishing domain takedowns are manual and time-consuming, often taking hours to days. Sentinel automates the detection and investigation process, compiling an evidence dossier and only requiring human intervention for the final, irreversible action.

The system employs a cost-effective cascade, where initial, cheaper layers discard approximately 99% of certificates before any token-costing LLMs are engaged. This design makes the process financially viable, with investigations costing roughly $0.001 each.

A key innovation is the detection of hidden Unicode Tag Characters embedded in phishing pages, specifically designed to mislead AI investigators. Sentinel records these attempts as strong signals of maliciousness, using them as primary evidence.

Scraped content, including text within images, is treated as adversarial and is never directly concatenated into prompts. The LLM's role is classification, not selecting the takedown recipient, which prevents attackers from redirecting notices.

During testing, a vulnerability was discovered in assuming RDAP output was inherently trustworthy, leading to a critical fix. This reinforced the principle that the source of data, whether a protocol or an LLM, does not inherently guarantee its security.
